lesson.title: Poles and Zeros: The Coordinates That Run the Show
lesson.summary: Poles and zeros are the complex frequency values where a transfer function blows up or vanishes, and their positions determine a circuit's frequency response and stability.
lesson.body:
A transfer function H(s) written as a ratio of two polynomials in the complex frequency variable s equals sigma plus j omega packs a circuit's entire frequency and time domain behavior into two short lists of numbers: the poles, which are the values of s that make the denominator zero, so H(s) grows without bound, and the zeros, which are the values of s that make the numerator zero, so H(s) itself vanishes. Because s is a complex number, poles and zeros generally come as complex values or as complex conjugate pairs, which is why a solid grip on complex numbers is essential before this material makes sense.

Start with the resistor capacitor low pass filter used throughout this unit, H(s) equals 1 over the quantity 1 plus sRC, with R equals 1000 ohms and C equals 0.1 microfarads, so RC equals 1 times 10 to the negative 4 seconds. Rewriting the denominator as s plus 1 over RC shows the pole sits where s equals negative 1 over RC, which is negative 10,000. Notice that the magnitude of this pole, 10,000 rad/s, is exactly the cutoff frequency computed earlier in this unit. That is not a coincidence: for a first order circuit, the pole's distance from the origin on the complex plane always equals its corner frequency. This filter has no zeros, since its numerator is just the constant 1.

Now take a series RLC circuit with the output measured across the resistor, which produces a band pass transfer function, H(s) equals (R over L) s, all over s squared plus (R over L) s plus 1 over LC. Using R equals 100 ohms, L equals 1 H, and C equals 1 microfarad from the bandwidth chapter, R over L equals 100 and 1 over LC equals 1,000,000. The numerator (R over L) s equals 100s is zero when s equals 0, so this circuit has one zero, sitting right at the origin. The poles come from solving s squared plus 100s plus 1,000,000 equals 0. The quadratic formula gives s equals the quantity negative 100 plus or minus the square root of (100 squared minus 4 times 1,000,000), all over 2, which is negative 100 plus or minus the square root of negative 3,990,000, over 2. Since the number under the square root is negative, the square root is imaginary: the square root of 3,990,000 is approximately 1997.5, so the poles are s equals (negative 100 plus or minus j 1997.5) over 2, which works out to approximately negative 50 plus or minus j 998.75.

These two poles are a complex conjugate pair, and each part carries meaning. The real part, negative 50, equals negative R over 2L, and it sets how quickly any transient in this circuit decays: the more negative it is, the faster the decay, and a negative real part is exactly what guarantees the circuit is stable rather than growing without bound. The imaginary part, approximately 998.75 rad/s, is the damped natural frequency at which the circuit actually rings.

The pole's distance from the origin turns out to equal omega_0 exactly, and this comes straight from the quadratic formula rather than from decimal rounding. The imaginary part was computed as the square root of omega_0 squared minus (R over 2L) squared. Squaring the real part gives (R over 2L) squared, and squaring the imaginary part gives omega_0 squared minus (R over 2L) squared; adding those two together, the (R over 2L) squared terms cancel, leaving just omega_0 squared. So the distance from the origin to the pole is the square root of omega_0 squared, which is omega_0 itself: 1000 rad/s for this circuit, the same undamped resonant frequency that the next few chapters build their entire treatment of quality factor, resonance, and series resonance around.
